```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Helpers: read saved tables and figures, and fail politely if they do not exist yet
tab_path <- function(f) here("outputs", "tables", f)
read_tab_df <- function(f) if (file.exists(tab_path(f))) read_csv(tab_path(f), show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL
show_tab <- function(f, digits = 3, caption = NULL) {
  d <- read_tab_df(f)
  if (is.null(d)) return(knitr::asis_output(paste0("*Table `", f, "` not found. Run the pipeline first.*")))
  kable(d, digits = digits, caption = caption)
}
show_fig <- function(folder, files) {
  p <- here("outputs", "figures", folder, files)
  ok <- file.exists(p)
  if (!any(ok)) return(knitr::asis_output("*Figures not found. Run the pipeline first.*"))
  knitr::include_graphics(p[ok])
}
```

# Abstract

*(Write this last, in 150 to 200 words.)* State, in this order: the problem (outbreak reports in India and what makes some outbreaks large), the data (EpiClim, 2009 to 2022), the methods (regression, classification, clustering, association rules), the main findings with your actual numbers, and the main limitation (event-based reports, weak climate signal).

# Introduction

## Background

Infectious diseases such as acute diarrhoeal disease, dengue, chikungunya, cholera and malaria cause recurring outbreaks across India. Climate conditions such as temperature, rainfall and vegetation are widely believed to influence outbreaks, but the strength of that relationship at district level is an empirical question.

## Problem statement

Given a reported outbreak in an Indian district, can we predict how large it will be, can we predict whether it will be unusually large for its disease, and which factors are associated with large outbreaks?

## Objectives

1. Analyse disease patterns across time, location and disease type, including seasonality.
2. Predict the size of reported outbreaks (case counts) using Multiple Linear Regression and Random Forest regression.
3. Predict whether a reported outbreak is a *surge* (unusually large for its disease) using Logistic Regression and Random Forest classification.
4. Identify the factors most associated with large outbreaks.
5. Discover recurring patterns using K-Means clustering and association rule mining.

## Scope note

The EpiClim records are **event-based**: a row exists only when an outbreak was reported. The data is not a continuous weekly surveillance series, so the project predicts the size of reported outbreaks, not the occurrence of outbreaks in a future week.

# Data

## Source and variables

The EpiClim dataset provides district-level outbreak reports from India with matching climate variables.

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `state_ut`, `district` | Location of the report |
| `Disease` | Disease name (22 raw labels, standardised in cleaning) |
| `Cases`, `Deaths` | Reported cases and deaths |
| `day`, `mon`, `year`, `week_of_outbreak` | Date fields and reporting week |
| `Latitude`, `Longitude` | Coordinates (grid-cell values, not district identifiers) |
| `Temp` | Temperature in Kelvin (converted to Celsius) |
| `preci` | Precipitation (units as defined in the EpiClim documentation) |
| `LAI` | Leaf area index (vegetation); scale to be confirmed from the documentation |

# Methodology

## Overall workflow

```
EpiClim raw data
      |
Cleaning  ->  Transformation / feature engineering
      |
Exploratory analysis  ->  Statistical analysis
      |
 +----+-----------------------------+
 |                                  |
Regression (log cases)       Classification (high outbreak)
 |                                  |
 +----------------+-----------------+
                  |
        Model evaluation + factor importance
                  |
     K-Means clustering  +  Association rules
                  |
         Final interpretation
```

## Data cleaning

- Removed the index column and exact duplicates.
- Converted `Cases` to numeric and removed rows that were non-numeric, zero or negative (a reported outbreak must have at least one case).
- Built a real date from day, month and year; kept the reporting week separately.
- Standardised disease names (22 labels merged into 8 groups) and dropped the handful of rows in the residual "Other" group.
- Tidied place names (removed corrupted characters and punctuation).
- Converted temperature from Kelvin to Celsius.
- Did **not** impute `Deaths` (about 72% missing); it is an outcome of the outbreak and is never used as a predictor.
- Flagged missing climate values; they are imputed later using training-set medians only.

## Feature engineering

- **Target for regression:** `log_cases = log(1 + Cases)`, because raw cases are extremely right-skewed.
- **Target for classification:** `high_outbreak` = `Cases` above the disease-specific 75th percentile, calculated from training years only.
- **Climate features:** temperature, log precipitation, leaf area index, with missing-value flags.
- **Time features:** month as sine and cosine, season, zone.
- **History features** (past reports of the same district and disease only): previous log cases, three-report rolling mean, days since previous report, number of prior reports.

## Train, test and stress split

| Set | Years | Purpose |
|-----|-------|---------|
| Train | 2009 to 2017 | Fit models, tune settings, compute thresholds and imputation values |
| Test | 2018 to 2019 | Final evaluation |
| Stress | 2020 to 2022 | Separate check; sparse and likely affected by COVID-era reporting |

A time-ordered split is used because predicting past years from future years would give misleadingly good results.

```{r split-table}
d <- if (file.exists(mod_p)) read_csv(mod_p, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL
if (!is.null(d)) kable(count(d, split, high_outbreak), caption = "Records by split and outbreak class")
```

## Models and evaluation

| Task | Models | Metrics |
|------|--------|---------|
| Regression | Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, disease-median baseline | RMSE, MAE, R-squared on the log scale |
| Classification | Logistic Regression, Random Forest, previous-report rule, always-Low | Precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC |
| Clustering | K-Means on district profiles | Elbow plot, average silhouette |
| Patterns | Apriori association rules | Support, confidence, lift |

Random Forest settings were tuned on a time-ordered validation slice inside the training years. Classification thresholds were chosen by maximising F1 on that validation slice, never on the test set.

# Model comparison and discussion

```{r headline, results = "asis"}
reg <- read_tab_df("regression_metrics.csv")
clf <- read_tab_df("classification_metrics.csv")
if (!is.null(reg)) {
  b <- reg %>% filter(set == "test", model != "Baseline") %>% arrange(RMSE) %>% slice(1)
  base <- reg %>% filter(set == "test", model == "Baseline")
  cat(sprintf("- **Regression:** best model on test years is **%s** (RMSE %.2f, R-squared %.2f); the disease-median baseline has RMSE %.2f.\n",
              b$model, b$RMSE, b$R2, base$RMSE))
}
if (!is.null(clf)) {
  b <- clf %>% filter(set == "test", !model %in% c("Always Low", "Previous report rule")) %>%
    arrange(desc(PR_AUC)) %>% slice(1)
  rule <- clf %>% filter(set == "test", model == "Previous report rule")
  cat(sprintf("- **Classification:** best model on test years is **%s** (PR-AUC %.2f, F1 %.2f, prevalence %.2f); the previous-report rule has PR-AUC %.2f.\n",
              b$model, b$PR_AUC, b$F1, b$prevalence, rule$PR_AUC))
}
```

> **Discussion:** *Answer each objective in one paragraph: what you found, how strong the evidence is, and what it means. Include the finding about climate even if it is weak.*

# Limitations

- Reports are event-based, so there is no information about periods without a reported outbreak, and week-ahead forecasting is not possible.
- Records from the same district are not independent, so p-values and intervals are indicative.
- District spelling variants may fragment history features and clusters.
- Reporting practices vary by state and over time; 2020 to 2022 is sparse and unusual.
- Climate variables are grid or satellite based and coarse; a share of leaf area index and temperature values were missing and imputed.
- Feature importance and association rules describe association, not causation.

- Use dense weekly surveillance data to forecast outbreak occurrence.
- Add spatial and hierarchical models that account for repeated reports from the same district.
- Merge district name variants with an authoritative district list.
